tracks.name: Frontend testing
tracks.blurb: Testing frontends with confidence: strategy, Vitest unit tests, React Testing Library, MSW, Playwright E2E, visual and performance tests, and fast CI without flaky tests.

lessons.title: Testing strategy: pyramid, trophy and what to test
lessons.summary: The test pyramid vs the testing trophy, deciding what is worth testing, and pushing each assertion to the cheapest layer that can catch the bug.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A test suite is a tool for changing code without fear. Every test buys some **confidence** that the product works, and every test has a **cost**: time to write, time to run, time to fix when it breaks for a reason that is not a bug. A testing strategy is just a deliberate answer to "where do we spend our test budget so that confidence per unit of cost is highest?"

Two failure modes are common. Teams with no strategy write whatever test is easiest (lots of shallow unit tests of trivial components, plus a few E2E scripts nobody trusts). Teams with a dogmatic strategy chase a number (100% coverage, "every component has a test file") and end up with suites that are slow, brittle and still miss real bugs. The goal is neither: it is a suite where a green build means "I would ship this", and a red build almost always means a real problem.

## The testing pyramid
Mike Cohn's test pyramid, popularised by Martin Fowler's "TestPyramid" bliki entry and Ham Vocke's "The Practical Test Pyramid" on martinfowler.com, says: write many fast, isolated unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few slow end-to-end (E2E) tests.

```text
            /\
           /E2E\         few: slow, broad, brittle, high confidence per test
          /------\
         /Integr. \      some: several units working together
        /----------\
       /    Unit    \    many: fast, isolated, cheap, narrow
      /--------------\
```

The reasoning was sound for the era it came from: E2E tests through a real browser were slow (minutes each) and flaky, while unit tests ran in milliseconds. Google's testing blog post "Just Say No to More End-to-End Tests" (2015) made the same case: an E2E failure tells you *something* is broken but not *what*, and the feedback loop is too long.

## The testing trophy
Kent C. Dodds' "testing trophy" reshapes this for frontend code, where the "unit" (a single component rendered with every child mocked) gives little confidence:

```text
          ___________
         |   E2E     |     a handful of critical journeys
         |___________|
        /             \
       /  Integration  \   most effort: a feature rendered with real children,
       \               /   real state, real hooks, network mocked at the edge
        \_____________/
           |  Unit  |      pure logic: formatters, reducers, validators
           |________|
          [  Static  ]     always on: TypeScript, ESLint
```

The key moves:
- **Static analysis is a layer.** TypeScript and ESLint catch a whole class of bugs (typos, wrong props, unhandled promise, missing hook dependency) for zero test code.
- **Integration is the fat middle.** Render a feature the way a user meets it (a checkout form with its real children and state), interact via roles and labels, and mock only the network. This is where frontend bugs live: wiring, state transitions, conditional rendering.
- **Unit tests are for pure logic**, not for "component renders a div".
- **E2E covers the money paths**: sign-in, checkout, publish. Few, but run against something close to production.

The slogan behind it, from Guillermo Rauch and amplified in Kent's "Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration.", is a reaction to suites full of shallow tests that break on refactors and never catch bugs.

Spotify's "testing honeycomb" (2018, for microservices) makes the same point from the backend side: integration tests that exercise a service through its real boundary give more value than piles of isolated unit tests.

Do not treat any shape as law. The right shape depends on where your bugs come from. A date-math library is unit-test heavy. A CRUD dashboard is integration heavy. A payments flow spanning three services needs a few real E2E tests no matter what.

## What to test
Ask of every candidate test: **"If this test fails, does it mean a user would see a bug?"** If not, it is probably testing an implementation detail.

Test:
- **User-visible behaviour**: what renders for each state (loading, empty, error, success), what happens on click, type, submit.
- **Business rules**: price calculation, permission checks, validation, date boundaries. These are the bugs that cost money.
- **Contracts at boundaries**: the shape of API responses you depend on, the props of a shared design-system component other teams consume.
- **Regressions**: every production bug gets a test that fails before the fix and passes after.
- **Accessibility basics**: elements have roles and names (querying by role tests this for free), automated axe checks on key pages.

Usually skip:
- Third-party library behaviour (React re-rendering, the router matching a path).
- Trivial markup with no logic.
- Private functions directly; test them through the public API that uses them.
- Exact CSS classes or internal state values. Kent C. Dodds' "Testing Implementation Details" defines the problem well: a test that breaks when you refactor without changing behaviour (a false negative) or passes when behaviour is broken (a false positive) is testing implementation details.

## Confidence vs cost, made concrete
Score a test on four axes:

| Axis | Unit | Integration (RTL + MSW) | E2E (Playwright) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Run time | ~1 ms | ~50-500 ms | ~2-30 s |
| Confidence per test | narrow | broad for one feature | whole system |
| Failure precision | exact line | one feature | "something is wrong" |
| Flake risk | very low | low | moderate to high |
| Refactor resilience | low if testing internals | high | high |

The numbers are rough orders of magnitude, not benchmarks; your machine and app decide the real values. The point is the ratios: one E2E test can cost as much CI time as hundreds of integration tests, so each one must protect something important.

A practical rule: **push each assertion to the cheapest layer that can still catch the bug.** "Discount codes are case-insensitive" is a unit test on the pricing function. "Applying a code updates the total shown" is an integration test. "A real user can pay with a card and receives an order confirmation" is E2E.

```ts
// Unit: pure rule, no React.
import { applyDiscount } from "./pricing";

test("discount codes are case-insensitive", () => {
  expect(applyDiscount(100, "save10")).toBe(90);
  expect(applyDiscount(100, "SAVE10")).toBe(90);
});
```

```tsx
// Integration: the feature as a user meets it, network mocked with MSW.
test("applying a code updates the total", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<Checkout />, { wrapper: AppProviders });
  await user.type(screen.getByRole("textbox", { name: /discount code/i }), "SAVE10");
  await user.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /apply/i }));
  expect(await screen.findByText("Total: $90.00")).toBeVisible();
});
```

```ts
// E2E: one journey through the real stack (Playwright).
test("guest can check out", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/products/blue-mug");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Add to cart" }).click();
  await page.getByRole("link", { name: "Checkout" }).click();
  // ...fill test card, submit
  await expect(page.getByRole("heading", { name: "Order confirmed" })).toBeVisible();
});
```

## Trade-offs and when not to follow the trophy
- **Very complex pure logic** (a spreadsheet formula engine, a rich-text diff) deserves dense unit and property-based tests regardless of trophy proportions.
- **Integration tests in jsdom** are not a real browser: no layout, no real focus behaviour in some cases, no `IntersectionObserver` without polyfills. For layout-sensitive components, use Vitest browser mode or Playwright component testing.
- **E2E against shared staging** environments is often flaky because data and deployments change under you. Prefer E2E against an ephemeral preview environment with seeded data.
- **Tests have a maintenance tax.** Deleting a low-value, frequently broken test is a legitimate improvement.

## Introducing a strategy to an untested codebase
1. Turn on the free layer: TypeScript `strict`, ESLint with `react-hooks` and `testing-library` plugins.
2. Write a smoke E2E test for the top 3 to 5 money journeys. This catches catastrophic breakage immediately.
3. Add an integration test whenever you touch a feature, and a regression test for every bug fix. Coverage grows where change happens, which is where risk is.
4. Extract business rules into pure functions as you go, and unit test them.
5. Track flake rate and suite duration from day one; a slow, flaky suite gets ignored.

## Common mistakes
- **Testing the mock.** A test that mocks every child and asserts the mock was called proves nothing about the product.
- **Shallow rendering** everything. It tests that you wrote the JSX you wrote.
- **Using coverage as the goal.** Coverage shows what is *unexecuted*; it cannot show what is *untested in a meaningful way*.
- **Writing E2E tests for edge cases** that an integration test could cover in a tenth of the time.
- **No test for the bug you just fixed**, so it comes back in six months.

## In the interview
What they probe: whether you have a reasoned position (not a slogan), whether you understand cost as well as confidence, and whether you can apply it to a messy real codebase.

Model 60-second answer outline:
1. "Tests buy confidence to change code; I spend the budget where confidence per cost is highest."
2. Pyramid vs trophy: static analysis always, most effort in integration tests that render real features with the network mocked, unit tests for pure logic, a few E2E tests for critical journeys.
3. "What to test": user-visible behaviour, business rules, contracts, every regression. Avoid implementation details.
4. Push each assertion to the cheapest layer that can catch the bug.
5. Mention that the shape depends on where bugs come from, and that flake rate and suite time are first-class metrics.

Follow-ups to expect: "How would you start on a codebase with no tests?", "When is a unit test better than an integration test?", "How do you stop the E2E suite becoming slow and flaky?", "What would you not test?"
keyPoints: A test buys confidence and costs time to write, run and maintain; strategy is where you spend that budget.
The trophy: static analysis always, most effort in integration tests, unit tests for pure logic, few E2E tests.
Ask of every test: if it fails, would a user see a bug? If not, it likely tests implementation details.
Push each assertion to the cheapest layer that can still catch the bug.
On an untested codebase: strict types and lint, smoke E2E for money paths, then tests where code changes.
interview: What is the testing pyramid, and how does the testing trophy differ from it?
How do you decide what to test and what not to test in a frontend codebase?
How would you introduce a testing strategy to a large frontend codebase that has almost no tests?

check.q: Under the testing trophy, where should most frontend test effort usually go?
options: Shallow-rendered unit tests of each component
Integration tests that render a feature with real children and mock only the network
End-to-end tests for every user flow
Snapshot tests of every page
check.why: Integration tests exercise the wiring, state and rendering where frontend bugs live, while staying fast and resilient to refactors.

check.q: You need to verify that discount codes are case-insensitive. Which layer is the cheapest that still catches the bug?
options: An E2E test through checkout
A visual regression test
A unit test of the pricing function
A manual QA script
check.why: The rule is pure logic, so a millisecond unit test on the pricing function catches it precisely; heavier layers add cost without extra confidence.

check.q: Which test is most likely testing an implementation detail?
options: Asserting the error message appears after submitting an invalid email
Asserting the total updates after applying a coupon
Asserting a modal can be closed with Escape
Asserting a component's internal isOpen state variable becomes true
check.why: Internal state is invisible to users; the test breaks on refactors that keep behaviour identical and can pass when the UI is broken.

lessons.title: Unit testing with Vitest: pure functions, time and coverage
lessons.summary: How Vitest runs tests, writing deterministic table-driven unit tests, controlling time with fake timers, and why coverage numbers mislead.
keyPoints: If code is hard to unit test, split the pure decision from the effect and test the decision densely.
Table-driven tests that hit boundaries catch more bugs than many tests of random middle values.
Inject now where you can; otherwise use vi.useFakeTimers, advanceTimersByTime and setSystemTime.
Coverage measures execution, not verification: check branches, include unimported files, never chase 100%.
Vitest reuses the Vite transform pipeline and a Jest-compatible API, so TS, ESM and aliases just work.
interview: What makes a function easy to unit test, and how would you test code that depends on time?
Why is 100% code coverage a poor goal, and what would you measure instead?
Why would you choose Vitest over Jest for a new project, and what changes when you migrate?

check.q: A debounced callback awaits a promise inside the timer. Your test advances fake timers but the follow-up assertion fails. What is the likely fix?
options: Switch to real timers and add a sleep
Use vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync so promise callbacks are flushed between timers
Call vi.resetModules() before the test
Increase the test timeout
check.why: The sync variant fires the timer but the awaited continuation runs on the microtask queue; the async variant flushes it.

check.q: Why can a suite with 95% line coverage still miss serious bugs?
options: Line coverage counts executed lines, not whether any assertion checked the result
Coverage tools cannot read TypeScript
Coverage only counts test files
The v8 provider ignores functions
check.why: A test can execute code and assert nothing; coverage shows what never ran, not what was meaningfully verified.

check.q: Which change makes isTrialActive(trial) easiest to test deterministically?
options: Read Date.now() inside a try/catch
Cache the current date in a module-level variable
Change the signature to isTrialActive(trial, now) and pass the time in
Use a 1-second setTimeout before checking
check.why: Injecting the clock makes the function pure, so tests pass explicit times without faking globals.

lessons.title: Component tests with React Testing Library
lessons.summary: Testing React components the way users use them: role queries, user-event, async utilities, act warnings, testing hooks, and the limits of jsdom.
keyPoints: Query by role and accessible name first, then label and text; test ids are the escape hatch.
getBy throws when missing, queryBy returns null for absence checks, findBy waits for async UI.
Use user-event (awaited, set up before render) instead of fireEvent to simulate full interactions.
An act warning usually means an update happened after the test stopped waiting; await the final UI state.
Test hooks through components by default; use renderHook for reusable hooks and read result.current fresh.
interview: Why does React Testing Library recommend querying by role, and what is the query priority?
What is the difference between getBy, queryBy and findBy, and when do you use each?
How do you test a custom React hook, and when should you test it through a component instead?
Why do you see 'not wrapped in act(...)' warnings, and how do you fix them properly?

check.q: You want to assert that an error banner is NOT shown. Which query is correct?
options: expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).toBeNull()
expect(await screen.findByRole('alert')).not.toBeInTheDocument()
expect(screen.queryByRole('alert')).not.toBeInTheDocument()
expect(screen.getAllByRole('alert')).toHaveLength(0)
check.why: queryBy returns null when nothing matches; getBy and getAllBy throw, and findBy rejects after its timeout.

check.q: A test passes but logs 'An update to OrdersPage inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)'. What is the best first fix?
options: Wrap the render call in act()
Await the final UI state, for example await screen.findByText('Saved'), so the test waits for the update
Silence console.error in the setup file
Switch from user-event to fireEvent
check.why: The warning means state changed after the test stopped waiting; awaiting the resulting UI both fixes the warning and makes the test assert the real outcome.

check.q: Why does getByRole('button', { name: /save/i }) fail to find a div with an onClick handler and the text Save?
options: Because the div is not exposed as a button in the accessibility tree
Because RTL ignores elements with event handlers
Because name matching is case-sensitive
Because getByRole only searches inside forms
check.why: Role queries use the accessibility tree; a div has no button role, so assistive technology users would not find it either.

lessons.title: Mocking boundaries, test doubles and MSW
lessons.summary: What to mock and why, the vocabulary of test doubles, mocking the network with MSW 2 in Node and the browser, and how to spot over-mocking.
keyPoints: Mock what is slow, non-deterministic or outside your control; every mock encodes an assumption.
Mock at boundaries (network, time, randomness, vendor SDKs), not your own modules or child components.
MSW intercepts requests at the network layer, so fetch, data hooks and error handling run for real.
Assert on UI outcomes rather than on requests; validate request bodies inside handlers instead.
Keep mocks honest with typed fixtures, contract tests and a few E2E runs against the real backend.
interview: What is the difference between a mock, a stub, a spy and a fake?
Why mock the network with MSW instead of mocking fetch or your API module?
How do you know when you are over-mocking, and what problems does it cause?

check.q: What does server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }) protect against?
options: Handlers returning slow responses
Tests silently making requests that no handler covers, possibly to a real API
Memory leaks in the Service Worker
Requests made with XMLHttpRequest
check.why: Any request without a matching handler fails loudly, so missing mocks are caught instead of hitting the network.

check.q: Which is an example of a fake rather than a stub?
options: vi.fn().mockReturnValue(42)
vi.spyOn(console, 'warn')
An onClose prop the test never calls
An in-memory orders store behind MSW handlers that supports create, list and refund
check.why: A fake is a working simplified implementation with behaviour and state; a stub only returns canned answers.

check.q: Your team mocks the api.ts module in every component test. What bug class is most likely to slip through?
options: Wrong URL building, serialisation or status handling inside the API client
CSS layout bugs
TypeScript type errors
Slow test runs
check.why: Mocking the module skips the client code itself; MSW keeps that code in the test path and fakes only the HTTP response.

lessons.title: End-to-end testing with Playwright
lessons.summary: Playwright locators and auto-waiting, fixtures, reusing auth state, parallel and sharded runs, and debugging failures with the trace viewer.
keyPoints: Keep E2E to critical journeys against a production-like build with seeded, per-test data.
Locators are lazy and strict; actions auto-wait for visible, stable, enabled elements, so never sleep.
Web-first assertions like await expect(locator).toBeVisible() retry until the condition holds.
Log in once in a setup project and reuse storageState; use one account per worker if tests mutate it.
Isolated browser contexts enable parallel workers and CI sharding; traces on first retry explain failures.
interview: How does Playwright's auto-waiting work, and why does it reduce flakiness compared to manual sleeps?
How do you handle authentication in a Playwright suite without logging in through the UI in every test?
How would you design an end-to-end test suite that stays fast and reliable as the product grows?

check.q: Why is expect(await page.getByText('Saved').isVisible()).toBe(true) worse than await expect(page.getByText('Saved')).toBeVisible()?
options: isVisible does not exist in Playwright
isVisible checks once immediately, while the web-first assertion retries until the timeout
toBeVisible ignores CSS
They behave identically
check.why: The web-first assertion waits for the UI to settle; the one-shot check races the render and causes flakes.

check.q: A click locator matches two Delete buttons on the page. What does Playwright do?
options: Clicks the first match
Clicks both
Clicks the last match
Throws a strict mode violation
check.why: Locators are strict for actions, forcing you to narrow the locator (for example by filtering to a row) instead of clicking the wrong element.

check.q: What does the recommended setup project for authentication save and reuse?
options: The browser's storage state (cookies and local storage) written to a file
The user's password in an environment variable only
A screenshot of the logged-in dashboard
A video of the login flow
check.why: The setup project logs in once and writes storageState; other projects load it so tests start already authenticated.

lessons.title: Visual regression testing
lessons.summary: Screenshot testing with Playwright and Storybook, hosted services like Chromatic, and the real engineering problem: making screenshots deterministic.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Functional tests check that the right elements exist and behave. They do not notice that the button is now white text on a white background, that a padding change pushed the price below the fold, or that a dependency upgrade changed every font weight. Visual regression testing does: it renders a page or component, takes a screenshot, and compares it pixel by pixel with an approved **baseline** image. Any difference beyond a threshold fails the test and shows a diff for a human to accept or reject.

The value is real (whole classes of CSS bugs are otherwise invisible to automation) but so is the cost: screenshots are sensitive to everything, so a naive setup produces a stream of false positives, and teams quickly learn to click "accept all". The engineering problem in visual testing is **determinism**.

## How it works step by step
```text
             +-----------------------+
 PR build -> | render story / page   |   fixed viewport, fonts, data, time
             +-----------+-----------+
                         |
                 screenshot (PNG)
                         |
             +-----------v-----------+      baseline from main
             | compare with baseline | <--- (stored in repo or SaaS)
             +-----------+-----------+
                         |
           diff <= threshold ?  ---- yes ---> pass
                         |
                         no
                         v
            fail + diff image (changed pixels highlighted)
                         |
         human reviews: bug -> fix code | intended -> update baseline
```

Three decisions define a setup:
1. **What to capture**: whole pages, or isolated components (usually Storybook stories). Components give precise, stable diffs; pages catch layout interactions between components.
2. **Where baselines live**: committed PNGs in the repo (Playwright snapshots) or a hosted service (Chromatic, Percy, Applitools) that stores baselines per branch and provides a review UI.
3. **How comparison works**: strict pixel diff with a tolerance, or perceptual or "visual AI" comparison offered by some commercial services.

## Playwright screenshot assertions
Playwright Test has visual comparison built in.

```ts
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("pricing page", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/pricing");
  await page.evaluate(() => document.fonts.ready);          // fonts loaded
  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot("pricing.png", {
    fullPage: true,
    mask: [page.getByTestId("live-visitor-count")],        // dynamic region painted over
    maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,                                // tolerate 1% of pixels changing
  });
});

test("primary button states", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/iframe.html?id=button--primary");      // a Storybook story
  const button = page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" });
  await expect(button).toHaveScreenshot("button-default.png");
  await button.hover();
  await expect(button).toHaveScreenshot("button-hover.png");
});
```

How it behaves:
- On the first run there is no baseline, so the test fails and writes one. Review it and commit it.
- `toHaveScreenshot` takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match (the page is stable), then compares with the baseline.
- By default it disables CSS animations and transitions and hides the text caret.
- Baseline file names include the browser and platform (for example `pricing-chromium-linux.png`), because rendering differs across operating systems.
- `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` regenerates baselines after an intended change.
- Tolerances: `maxDiffPixels` (absolute count), `maxDiffPixelRatio` (fraction), and `threshold` (how different a single pixel's colour must be to count, 0 to 1).

## Component-level visual testing with Storybook
Storybook stories are already a catalogue of every component state: default, hover, disabled, loading, error, long text, right-to-left, dark theme. That makes them ideal visual test cases: each story becomes a snapshot.

```tsx
// button.stories.tsx
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from "@storybook/react-vite";
import { Button } from "./button";

const meta: Meta<typeof Button> = { component: Button, args: { children: "Save" } };
export default meta;
type Story = StoryObj<typeof Button>;

export const Primary: Story = { args: { variant: "primary" } };
export const Disabled: Story = { args: { variant: "primary", disabled: true } };
export const LongLabel: Story = { args: { children: "Save changes and notify all collaborators" } };
export const Loading: Story = { args: { loading: true } };
```

Options:
- **Chromatic** (by the Storybook maintainers) uploads the built Storybook, snapshots every story in cloud browsers, keeps baselines per branch, and gives designers and engineers a review UI. TurboSnap uses git and the dependency graph to snapshot only stories affected by a change, which saves time and snapshot quota.
- **Self-hosted**: iterate over stories (from Storybook's generated `index.json`) and call Playwright's `toHaveScreenshot` for each, running inside the official Playwright Docker image so rendering is identical on every machine.

Hosted services cost money beyond free tiers but remove the hardest operational problems: consistent rendering, baseline storage per branch and a review workflow. Self-hosting is free but you own determinism and baseline churn.

## Flake control: making screenshots deterministic
Most visual test pain comes from these sources:

| Source of noise | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Different OS, GPU, font rendering | Run in one pinned Docker image (e.g. the official Playwright image matching your version) locally and in CI |
| Web fonts loading late | Self-host fonts, wait for `document.fonts.ready` |
| Animations, transitions, carets | Disabled by default in `toHaveScreenshot`; also honour `prefers-reduced-motion` in the app |
| Dates, "3 minutes ago", random data | Freeze the clock (`page.clock`), seed data, mock the network with MSW or `page.route` |
| Lazy images, skeletons | Wait for network idle on images or for the final element; disable lazy loading in test builds |
| Ads, live counters, avatars | `mask` the region, or replace with fixtures |
| Scrollbars, viewport size | Fixed viewport per project; hide scrollbars with an injected stylesheet |
| Anti-aliasing noise | Small tolerance (`threshold`, `maxDiffPixelRatio`), never a large one |

A large tolerance is a smell: a 5% pixel tolerance will happily accept a missing button. Keep tolerances tight and remove the noise at its source instead.

## Review workflow
The diff is only useful if someone looks at it:
- Make visual diffs a required PR check with an explicit "approve changes" step by the author or a designer.
- Keep snapshots small and named for the state they show so diffs are reviewable.
- Update baselines in the same PR as the change, never in a separate "update all snapshots" commit.
- With repo-stored baselines, generate them in CI's Docker image (or a script that runs the same image locally), not on a developer's Mac, or every baseline will differ by platform.

## Trade-offs and when not to use it
- Visual tests catch **unintended** visual change; they do not tell you whether a design is right. They complement, not replace, design review.
- They are poor at highly dynamic pages (feeds, dashboards with live data) unless you control the data completely.
- Full-page screenshots across many viewports and browsers multiply quickly: 200 stories x 3 viewports x 2 themes = 1,200 snapshots. Prioritise: design-system components in all themes, key pages at two viewports.
- For layout logic you can express in assertions (element is within viewport, no horizontal overflow), a functional assertion is cheaper and more precise.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- Generating baselines on a laptop and comparing on Linux CI.
- Raising the tolerance to silence flakes instead of fixing the cause.
- Huge page snapshots where any change anywhere fails the test.
- Accepting diffs without looking. If reviewers routinely accept everything, the suite is noise; fix determinism or reduce scope.
- Debugging: open the HTML report, which shows expected, actual and diff side by side; check whether the diff is everywhere (font or platform) or local (a real change).

## In the interview
What they probe: do you understand that the hard problem is determinism, and can you design a workflow people will actually use.

Model 60-second answer outline:
1. Visual tests compare screenshots to approved baselines and catch CSS regressions functional tests miss.
2. Capture at component level (Storybook stories as the catalogue of states) plus a few key pages.
3. Determinism: one pinned Docker image, loaded fonts, disabled animations, frozen time, mocked data, masked dynamic regions, tight tolerances.
4. Tooling: Playwright `toHaveScreenshot` with baselines in the repo, or a hosted service like Chromatic for per-branch baselines, review UI and TurboSnap.
5. Workflow: required check, designer-friendly review, baselines updated in the same PR.

Follow-ups to expect: "How do you handle a page with a live chart?", "Where would you store baselines?", "How do you keep snapshot counts manageable?", "What threshold would you choose and why?"
keyPoints: Visual tests compare screenshots against approved baselines and catch CSS regressions functional tests miss.
Storybook stories make an ideal catalogue of component states to snapshot; add a few key pages.
Determinism first: one pinned Docker image, loaded fonts, no animations, frozen time, mocked data, masks.
Keep tolerances tight; a large tolerance hides real bugs. Remove noise at its source instead.
Make diffs a required, reviewed PR check and update baselines in the same PR as the change.
interview: What is visual regression testing, and what makes screenshot tests flaky?
How would you set up visual regression testing for a component library?

check.q: Baselines were generated on a developer's Mac and every CI run on Linux now fails with small diffs everywhere. What is the right fix?
options: Raise maxDiffPixelRatio to 10%
Disable visual tests on CI
Generate and compare baselines in the same pinned Docker image everywhere
Switch to JPEG screenshots
check.why: Font rendering and anti-aliasing differ by OS; a single pinned environment makes rendering identical, while a big tolerance would hide real bugs.

check.q: Which is the best way to handle a live visitor counter inside a page snapshot?
options: Mask the counter region or replace its data with a fixture
Retry the test until it passes
Increase the threshold option to 0.9
Take the screenshot twice and keep the second
check.why: Masking or fixing the data removes the nondeterministic region while still comparing the rest of the page strictly.

check.q: What does Chromatic's TurboSnap do?
options: Compresses screenshots to save storage
Runs visual tests in WebKit only
Converts stories into Playwright tests
Snapshots only the stories affected by the code change, using git and the dependency graph
check.why: TurboSnap skips unaffected stories, cutting build time and snapshot usage on large libraries.

lessons.title: Performance testing: Lighthouse CI, budgets and k6
lessons.summary: Catching performance regressions in CI with Lighthouse CI and byte budgets, watching real users with web-vitals, and load testing APIs with k6.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Performance is a feature that regresses silently. Nobody files a bug when a page gets 300 ms slower; conversion just drops a little. Functional tests do not notice either. Performance testing turns "fast" into numbers with thresholds that fail a build, so regressions are caught in the pull request that caused them rather than in a quarterly audit.

For a frontend engineer there are three layers:
1. **Lab tests in CI**: run Lighthouse (or Playwright with throttling) against a build on every PR and assert on metrics and budgets.
2. **Field data in production**: real-user monitoring (RUM) of Core Web Vitals, the numbers that actually matter.
3. **Load tests on the APIs** the frontend depends on: a page cannot be faster than its slowest critical request under real traffic. k6 is the common tool.

## The metrics, briefly
Core Web Vitals, as defined on web.dev, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads:

| Metric | Measures | Good |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) | loading: when the main content appears | <= 2.5 s |
| INP (Interaction to Next Paint) | responsiveness to clicks, taps, keys | <= 200 ms |
| CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) | visual stability | <= 0.1 |

INP needs real user interactions, so lab tools cannot measure it directly. Total Blocking Time (TBT) in a Lighthouse run is the usual lab proxy: long main-thread tasks during load that would delay an interaction.

## Lab vs field
```text
            LAB (synthetic)                        FIELD (real users)
   one device profile, one network          thousands of devices, networks, caches
   reproducible, runs on every PR           noisy, but the truth
   Lighthouse, WebPageTest, Playwright      web-vitals library, CrUX, RUM vendor
   good for catching regressions            good for knowing actual user experience
   no INP (use TBT as proxy)                INP, LCP, CLS at p75
```

web.dev's "Why lab and field data can be different" explains the common causes: real users have slower phones, warm or cold caches, logged-in states, different viewports (so a different LCP element), and they interact during load. A page can score 98 in Lighthouse on a CI machine and still fail LCP at p75 in the field. Use lab tests to **detect change** and field data to **judge quality**.

## Lighthouse CI
Lighthouse CI (`@lhci/cli`) runs Lighthouse several times against URLs, asserts on the results and can upload reports.

```js
// lighthouserc.js
module.exports = {
  ci: {
    collect: {
      startServerCommand: "npm run start",
      url: ["http://localhost:3000/", "http://localhost:3000/products/blue-mug"],
      numberOfRuns: 3, // Lighthouse results vary run to run; assert on an aggregate
    },
    assert: {
      assertions: {
        "categories:performance": ["error", { minScore: 0.9, aggregationMethod: "median-run" }],
        "largest-contentful-paint": ["error", { maxNumericValue: 2500 }],
        "total-blocking-time": ["warn", { maxNumericValue: 200 }],
        "cumulative-layout-shift": ["error", { maxNumericValue: 0.1 }],
        "resource-summary:script:size": ["error", { maxNumericValue: 300000 }],
      },
    },
    upload: { target: "temporary-public-storage" },
  },
};
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/perf.yml (excerpt)
- run: npm ci && npm run build
- run: npx @lhci/cli autorun
```

Practical notes:
- **Variance is the enemy.** CI runners are shared and noisy. Run 3 to 5 times and assert on the median, keep thresholds with headroom, and treat small fluctuations as noise. Some teams run Lighthouse on a dedicated machine for stable numbers.
- **Test production builds**, never the dev server (unminified, no code splitting, extra dev-only checks).
- **Pick representative URLs**: the landing page, a heavy product or dashboard page, and a page with a large image.
- Lighthouse throttles CPU and network to simulate a mid-range phone on a slow connection by default. That is intentional; desktop-unthrottled numbers flatter you.

## Performance budgets
A performance budget is a limit agreed in advance: "the product page ships at most 170 KB of compressed JavaScript", "LCP at most 2.5 s on the lab profile", "no more than 50 requests". web.dev's "Performance budgets 101" distinguishes quantity-based budgets (bytes, requests), milestone timings (LCP, TTI) and rule-based (Lighthouse score).

Byte budgets are the most stable in CI because they do not vary between runs. The `size-limit` tool checks the compressed size of each entry point and fails the PR if it grows past the limit:

```json
[
  { "path": ".next/static/chunks/app/page-*.js", "limit": "120 kB" },
  { "path": "dist/widget.js", "limit": "15 kB", "gzip": true }
]
```

Report the delta on the PR ("+18 kB: added date-fns locale"), so the author sees the cost of an import while the change is fresh. That feedback loop matters more than the absolute number.

## Field monitoring
In production, collect Core Web Vitals from real users with the `web-vitals` library and send them to your analytics or RUM backend:

```ts
import { onCLS, onINP, onLCP } from "web-vitals";

function send(metric: { name: string; value: number; id: string; rating: string }) {
  navigator.sendBeacon("/rum", JSON.stringify({ ...metric, path: location.pathname }));
}

onLCP(send);
onINP(send);
onCLS(send);
```

Dashboard the p75 per route and per device class, and alert on regressions after deploys. The Chrome UX Report (CrUX) provides public 28-day field data for sites with enough traffic; it is what Google Search uses for its page experience signals.

## Load testing APIs with k6
A frontend's LCP is often bounded by an API call (the product data, the feed). If that endpoint degrades from 80 ms to 2 s at peak traffic, no amount of bundle optimisation helps. k6 (by Grafana Labs) scripts load tests in JavaScript and runs them from a Go engine.

```js
// load-products.js  (run: k6 run -e BASE_URL=$STAGING_URL load-products.js)
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    browse: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate", // open model: fixed requests per second
      rate: 200,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "5m",
      preAllocatedVUs: 100,
      maxVUs: 400,
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300", "p(99)<800"], // ms
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"],
    checks: ["rate>0.99"],
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/api/products?page=1`);
  check(res, { "status 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}
```

Key ideas:
- **Thresholds turn a load test into a pass or fail check** that CI can gate on (k6 exits non-zero when a threshold fails).
- **Open vs closed models.** Closed-model executors (a fixed number of virtual users looping) slow down when the system slows down, because each user waits for its response before sending the next. That under-reports latency under overload (the coordinated omission problem). Arrival-rate executors keep sending at the target rate, like real independent users. k6's docs on open and closed models explain the difference.
- **Test types**: smoke (tiny load, does it work), load (expected peak), stress (beyond peak, where does it break), spike (sudden surge), soak (hours at normal load, to find leaks).
- **Measure percentiles, not averages.** An average of 120 ms can hide a p99 of 3 s.
- **Never load test production or third parties without agreement**; use a production-like staging environment with realistic data volume, or you test an empty database's cache.

## Trade-offs
- Lighthouse scores are a composite and change between Lighthouse versions; assert on specific metrics and byte budgets, not only the score.
- Lab tests catch regressions, not real-world slowness; pair with field RUM.
- Load tests are expensive to run on every PR; run a smoke version per PR and full load tests nightly or before launches.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- Running Lighthouse once and failing builds on noise, so the team disables the check.
- Measuring the dev server.
- Budgets with no owner: when the budget fails, someone must decide (optimise, or consciously raise the budget with a reason).
- Load testing with a closed model and concluding latency is fine under overload.
- To debug a lab regression, compare the two Lighthouse reports: the treemap shows which script grew; the performance trace shows the new long task.

## In the interview
What they probe: whether you know lab vs field, can set up automated guards, and understand the backend side of frontend speed.

Model 60-second answer outline:
1. Define metrics: Core Web Vitals at p75 (LCP 2.5 s, INP 200 ms, CLS 0.1); TBT as the lab proxy for INP.
2. In CI: Lighthouse CI on production builds, multiple runs, median, assertions on specific metrics; byte budgets with size-limit and PR deltas.
3. In production: web-vitals RUM per route and device, alert on post-deploy regressions.
4. APIs: k6 with arrival-rate scenarios and percentile thresholds, smoke per PR, full load nightly.
5. Close with lab-vs-field differences and why both are needed.

Follow-ups to expect: "Lighthouse says 95 but users complain; why?", "How do you stop flaky perf checks?", "What is coordinated omission?", "How would you budget a third-party script?"
keyPoints: Lab tests detect change on every PR; field RUM data tells you what users actually experience.
Run Lighthouse CI on production builds several times and assert on specific metrics, not one noisy score.
Byte budgets (size-limit) are stable in CI; report the delta on the PR so authors see the cost.
Load test critical APIs with k6 arrival-rate scenarios and percentile thresholds that fail the run.
Closed-model load tests under-report latency under overload; use open models for realistic traffic.
interview: How do you prevent performance regressions from reaching production?
Lab data says the page is fast but field data says it is slow. How do you explain and resolve that?
How would you load test an API that your frontend depends on, and what would you measure?

check.q: Why can't a Lighthouse run in CI measure INP directly?
options: INP is only available in Firefox
INP requires real user interactions; lab runs use TBT as a proxy
Lighthouse disables JavaScript
INP is measured only on the server
check.why: INP observes actual interactions across a visit; Lighthouse load runs have none, so Total Blocking Time approximates main-thread blocking.

check.q: Which perf check is least affected by CI machine noise?
options: A single Lighthouse performance score
LCP from one run
Total Blocking Time from one run
A compressed JavaScript size budget per entry point
check.why: Bundle size is deterministic for a given build, while timing metrics vary with shared runner load.

check.q: In k6, why prefer a constant-arrival-rate executor for testing behaviour under overload?
options: It keeps sending requests at the target rate even when responses slow, avoiding coordinated omission
It uses fewer virtual users in every case
It disables thresholds
It only runs in the browser module
check.why: Closed models wait for each response, so they send less traffic when the system slows and hide the latency real users would see.

lessons.title: CI pipelines, sharding and flaky tests
lessons.summary: Designing a fast frontend CI pipeline, sharding long suites, finding the cause of flaky tests, and a retry and quarantine policy that keeps trust.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Tests only protect you if they run on every change and their result is trusted. Two things destroy that: **slow pipelines** (developers stop waiting and merge anyway, or batch huge PRs) and **flaky tests** (tests that pass and fail on the same code). Once a team learns that "red probably means flaky, just rerun", real failures get rerun into green and shipped.

Martin Fowler's "Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests" calls non-deterministic tests a virulent infection that can ruin a suite. Google's testing blog post "Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them" (2016) reported about 1.5% of all test runs giving a flaky result and almost 16% of their tests showing some flakiness. At that scale, flakiness is not an occasional annoyance; it is a constant tax that needs a policy.

## A good frontend pipeline
```text
PR opened / pushed
   |
   +-- install (cached by lockfile hash)
   |
   +-- parallel fast lane (minutes) ---------------------------+
   |     typecheck   lint   unit + component tests (Vitest)    |
   |     build       bundle size budget                        |
   +-----------------------------------------------------------+
   |
   +-- slower lane (on the built artefact)
   |     E2E Playwright, sharded 4 ways
   |     visual regression     Lighthouse CI
   |
   +-- merge results -> required checks -> merge queue -> deploy
```

Principles:
- **Fail fast**: the cheap checks (types, lint, unit) run first or in parallel and give feedback in a few minutes.
- **Build once, test the artefact**: E2E, visual and Lighthouse all run against the same production build, not a dev server.
- **Cache aggressively**: dependency install keyed on the lockfile, the Playwright browser download, and build outputs. Monorepo tools (Turborepo, Nx) cache task results and can run only tasks affected by the change.
- **Parallelise and shard**: split long suites across machines.
- **Make required checks meaningful**: if a check is often ignored, fix it or remove it.

## Sharding
Sharding splits a test suite across several CI machines, each running a fraction.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4]
        shardTotal: [4]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        with:
          name: blob-report-${{ matrix.shardIndex }}
          path: blob-report
          retention-days: 1
```

With the Playwright `blob` reporter configured on CI, a follow-up job downloads all shard artefacts and runs `npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports` to produce one report. Vitest supports `--shard=1/3` too.

Sharding has overhead per machine (checkout, install, browser download, app start), so going from 4 to 16 shards rarely gives 4x. Balance matters: with `fullyParallel: true`, Playwright shards at test level rather than file level, which gives more even shards.

## What makes tests flaky
Fowler groups the causes; in frontend suites they look like this:

| Cause | Frontend example | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Async timing | asserting before a fetch resolves; `waitForTimeout(500)` | web-first assertions, `findBy`, await the final state |
| Shared state / order dependence | test B relies on data test A created; leaked mocks | per-test data, reset handlers and mocks, isolated contexts |
| Time | "expires today" fails after midnight UTC | inject or freeze the clock; set `TZ` |
| Randomness | random IDs or shuffled lists in assertions | seed or inject generators |
| External services | real third-party API in E2E | fake at the boundary or use a sandbox with retries in the fixture, not the test |
| Resource limits | CI machine slower, timeouts too tight | sensible timeouts, fewer workers on small runners |
| Animations, layout | clicking an element mid-transition | Playwright actionability waits; disable animations in test builds |
| Real app races | double-submit, stale responses overwriting fresh ones | fix the app; the test found a real bug |

The last row matters: a meaningful share of "flaky tests" are real race conditions that users also hit, just rarely.

## Investigating a flaky test
1. **Reproduce under stress**: `npx playwright test my.spec.ts --repeat-each=50 --workers=4`, or Vitest with `--sequence.shuffle` and repeated runs. Add CPU pressure or run on the same runner size as CI.
2. **Get evidence from CI**: traces on first retry, screenshots, videos, console and network logs. The trace usually shows the page state at the failing step.
3. **Check isolation**: does it fail only when run with other tests? Run it alone, then with its file, then in shuffled order. That points to shared state.
4. **Check time and environment**: timezone, locale, date near midnight, viewport size, fonts.
5. **Fix the cause**, not the symptom. Replacing a sleep with a longer sleep is not a fix.

## Retries: useful, dangerous
Retries (`retries: 2` in Playwright on CI, the `retry` option in Vitest) stop one flaky test from blocking every PR. Playwright marks a test that failed and then passed as **flaky** in the report, rather than plain passed.

The danger is that retries hide flakiness indefinitely and can hide real intermittent bugs. Guard rails:
- Track flaky results as a metric (per test, over time), not just pass/fail.
- Retries on CI only, never locally, so developers see the flake.
- A test that needs retries regularly goes into quarantine and gets an owner.

## Quarantine
Quarantine moves a known-flaky test out of the blocking path while keeping it running, so it neither blocks merges nor disappears.

```ts
test("bulk export finishes", { tag: "@quarantine" }, async ({ page }) => {
  // ...
});
```

```bash
npx playwright test --grep-invert @quarantine   # blocking job
npx playwright test --grep @quarantine          # non-blocking job, results tracked
```

A workable policy:
1. Auto-detect: a test that fails then passes on retry, or fails on main without a related change, is flagged. Slack Engineering's post "Handling Flaky Tests at Scale: Auto Detection and Suppression" describes automating exactly this.
2. Quarantine within a day, with a ticket and a named owner.
3. Fix or delete within a fixed window (for example two weeks). A quarantined test nobody fixes provides no protection; delete it and write a better one.
4. Never quarantine without tracking; an ever-growing quarantine list is just a slow deletion.

## Test data
Unreliable data is the biggest source of E2E flakiness.
- **Create, do not share**: each test creates what it needs via an API or factory, with unique names (`project-${testInfo.workerIndex}-${Date.now()}`), and cleans up in fixture teardown.
- **Seeded, disposable environments**: a fresh database per CI run (a container or a branch database) seeded with fixed reference data.
- **Factories over fixtures files**: `buildUser({ role: "admin" })` with sensible defaults keeps tests short and expresses intent.
- **No dependence on production-like copies** with personal data; generate synthetic data.
- **Test-only endpoints** for setup (`/api/test/reset`) must be disabled in production builds.

## Trade-offs
- More shards cost more CI minutes; per-PR you might run Chromium sharded and run Firefox and WebKit nightly.
- Running only "affected" tests speeds PRs but can miss indirect breakage; run the full suite on main and before release.
- Merge queues (test the PR rebased on the latest main before merging) prevent "green PR, red main" at the cost of queue time.

## Common mistakes
- Treating rerun-until-green as normal.
- Retries enabled locally, so nobody notices flakes until CI.
- A single shared test account mutated by parallel tests.
- No artefacts on failure, so every CI flake requires a local repro.
- Slow pipelines accepted as a fact of life; measure duration and set a target (for example under 10 minutes to a mergeable signal).

## In the interview
What they probe: a concrete debugging process, a policy with ownership, and practical CI speed techniques.

Model 60-second answer outline:
1. Flaky tests destroy trust; real failures get rerun to green. Track flake rate as a metric.
2. Common causes: async timing, shared state, time, randomness, external services, real app races.
3. Investigate: repeat under stress, use CI traces, check isolation and environment, fix the cause.
4. Policy: retries on CI only and reported as flaky; auto-detect; quarantine with owner and deadline; fix or delete.
5. Speed: fail-fast lane, build once, caching, affected-only runs, sharding with merged reports, per-test data.

Follow-ups to expect: "How do you decide between fixing and deleting a flaky test?", "How would you shard a suite with uneven test durations?", "How do you keep test data isolated in parallel runs?", "What would you measure about the pipeline?"
keyPoints: Slow pipelines and flaky tests both destroy trust; once red means rerun, real bugs ship.
Fail fast with cheap checks, build once and test the artefact, cache installs and browsers, shard long suites.
Most flakes come from async timing, shared state, time, randomness or external services; some are real app races.
Retries on CI only, reported as flaky; quarantine with an owner and a deadline, then fix or delete.
Each test creates its own uniquely named data in a seeded, disposable environment.
interview: A test fails 1 in 20 runs on CI but never locally. How do you investigate it?
What is your policy for flaky tests: retry, quarantine or delete?
How would you cut a 40-minute frontend CI pipeline down to under 10 minutes?

check.q: A Playwright test fails on the first attempt and passes on retry. How does Playwright report it?
options: As passed, with no record of the failure
As failed
As flaky
As skipped
check.why: Playwright distinguishes flaky tests (failed then passed on retry) so you can track them instead of hiding them.

check.q: A test passes alone but fails when run with the rest of its file. What is the most likely cause?
options: Shared state or order dependence between tests, such as leaked mocks or reused data
The browser version is too new
The test timeout is too long
Sharding is disabled
check.why: Failing only in combination points to state left behind by earlier tests; isolate data and reset mocks and handlers.

check.q: What is the main purpose of quarantining a flaky test rather than deleting it immediately?
options: To hide it permanently from reports
To make the pipeline run it more often in the blocking job
To avoid assigning an owner
To stop it blocking merges while it keeps running and gets fixed by an owner within a deadline
check.why: Quarantine removes the merge-blocking pain but keeps visibility and accountability; without a deadline it decays into silent deletion.

projects.title: Full-stack testing harness for a React app
projects.summary: A small but real React app (auth, projects, checkout) wrapped in a complete test system: unit, component, network-mocked integration, E2E, visual, accessibility and performance tests, run by a sharded CI pipeline that measures and quarantines flaky tests.
projects.why: Most candidates say they write tests; few can show a suite designed on purpose. This project demonstrates judgement (what to test at which layer), the engineering behind reliable suites (typed mocks, isolated data, deterministic screenshots) and CI skills (sharding, caching, flake tracking). A hiring manager can open the pipeline, the merged Playwright report and the flake dashboard and see senior-level thinking about quality and developer experience.
projects.architecture:
```text
                    apps/web (Next.js or Vite + React)
   +-------------------------------------------------------------+
   |  pages: login, projects list, project detail, checkout      |
   |  data layer: typed API client (generated from OpenAPI)      |
   +---------------+-------------------------------+-------------+
                   |                               |
         MSW handlers (shared)              real API (apps/api)
      packages/test-kit/handlers           Postgres, seeded per run
                   |                               |
   +---------------v-------------+   +-------------v---------------+
   | Vitest: unit + RTL tests    |   | Playwright E2E (sharded x4) |
   | Storybook stories + a11y    |   | setup project -> auth state |
   | visual snapshots (Docker)   |   | Lighthouse CI, k6 smoke     |
   +---------------+-------------+   +-------------+---------------+
                   \                               /
                    +---- GitHub Actions pipeline +
                         fast lane -> slow lane -> merged report
                         flake tracker -> quarantine job
```

Key decisions:
- **One source of truth for API shapes**: an OpenAPI schema generates client types and types the MSW handlers, so mocks cannot drift silently.
- **Shared test kit package** (`packages/test-kit`): factories, MSW handlers, render helpers and Playwright fixtures used by every layer.
- **Build once**: E2E, visual and Lighthouse all run against the same production artefact.
- **Flakiness is data**: every CI run uploads JUnit and Playwright JSON results; a small script computes per-test flake rates and drives quarantine.

Generate TypeScript types from an OpenAPI schema and use them in the API client
Create packages/test-kit with data factories and typed MSW handlers

milestones.title: E2E suite with isolated data

Write fixtures that create and delete per-test data through test-only API routes
Cover the five critical journeys with role-based locators and web-first assertions only

Run axe checks on stories and on key E2E pages with @axe-core/playwright

milestones.title: Performance guards

Add size-limit budgets with the delta posted on the PR

milestones.title: Fast sharded CI pipeline
details: Split CI into a fast lane (typecheck, lint, Vitest, build) and a slow lane on the built artefact
Shard Playwright four ways with the blob reporter and merge into one HTML report
Cache installs and Playwright browsers keyed by lockfile

What made screenshots flaky and how the pinned Docker image, fonts and frozen time fixed it

deepDives.title: Keeping mocks honest with types generated from the API schema
Isolated test data for parallel E2E runs
Measuring flakiness and automating quarantine
deepDives.body:
Retries keep CI green but hide flakiness. The project treats flakiness as measured data rather than a feeling.

**Pipeline**: Vitest writes JUnit XML and Playwright writes its JSON report on every run on `main` and on PRs. A small Node script appends one row per test result (test id, outcome, retry count, commit, duration) to a results store (a JSON file artefact or a SQLite file is enough for a portfolio project).

**Flake score**: over the last N runs on `main`, a test is flaky if it has both passes and failures on the same commit, or passed only after a retry. The score is the share of runs where that happened.

```text
flake_rate(test) = runs_with(fail_then_pass or mixed_on_same_commit) / total_runs
quarantine if flake_rate > 2% over the last 50 runs
```

**Automation**: tests above the threshold get a `@quarantine` tag added by a bot PR, with an issue assigned to the last author of the test file. The blocking job runs `--grep-invert @quarantine`; a non-blocking job runs only quarantined tests and records results. A test that stays quarantined past 14 days is flagged for deletion.

**Trade-off**: thresholds are arbitrary and too low a threshold quarantines tests that failed once due to infrastructure. Separate infrastructure failures (runner crashed, install failed) from test failures before scoring.

deepDives.title: Deterministic visual snapshots
deepDives.body:
Visual tests are only worth having if diffs are real. The project renders every Storybook story in each theme and compares screenshots, and the core design work is removing noise.

**Determinism checklist applied in the harness**:
- All screenshots are taken inside the official Playwright Docker image pinned to the same version as `@playwright/test`, locally (via a `npm run test:visual` script that wraps `docker run`) and in CI.
- Fonts are self-hosted and the harness waits for `document.fonts.ready` before capturing.
- A global decorator freezes dates and seeds any random data; network data comes from the shared MSW handlers.
- Animations are disabled by `toHaveScreenshot` and by honouring `prefers-reduced-motion` in components.
- Tolerance is tight (`maxDiffPixelRatio` around 0.001 per component) and never raised to fix a flake.

**Scope control**: design-system components in light and dark themes, plus three full pages at mobile and desktop widths. Changed-file detection skips stories whose component files and imports did not change on a PR, and the full set runs on `main`.

**Trade-off**: committing PNG baselines to git grows the repo; Git LFS or a hosted service solves that at the cost of setup or money. For a portfolio project, committed baselines in a separate folder are acceptable and transparent to reviewers.
